rem:poisson-hkr-connection:
Remark HKR and skew-Poisson integration. The internal Poisson object makes explicit a structure implicit in the deformation theory. Over \mathbf{C} = \mathrm{Mod}(\mathbb{F}_p) with A = \mathcal{O}(H), the analogous structure is the Poisson structure of the skew-Poisson integration theorem, stated in the chapter on models of quantum observable universes.

From Hochschild to bivectors. The first-order deformation \phi_1 \in HH^2(A, A) of the Frobenius--Hopf algebra A maps under the Hochschild--Kostant--Rosenberg isomorphism to a bivector field:

\mathrm{HKR} \colon HH^2(A, A)
\xrightarrow{ \sim }
\Gamma\!\bigl(\Lambda^2 T_A\bigr)
= 
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{C}}\!\bigl(\mathbf{1},
  \Lambda^2(\Omega^1(A)^{\vee})\bigr).

The image \pi := \mathrm{HKR}(\phi_1) is a global section of the bivector object \Pi. The Jacobi identity on \pi corresponds to the Maurer--Cartan equation [\phi_1, \phi_1] = 0.

Internal vs. external. The classical approach defines the Poisson bracket by passing through \tau to the vector-space level and invoking HKR. The internal definition avoids this detour. The bivector \pi \colon \mathbf{1} \to \Pi and the contraction live entirely inside \mathbf{C}.

Model: skew-Poisson integration. When \mathbf{C} = \mathrm{Mod}(\mathbb{F}_p) and A = \mathcal{O}(H), the comparison is with the Poisson structure of the skew-Poisson integration theorem: a bracket on a splay of one-dimensional distribution algebras that vanishes on each factor and is strongly filtered. Whether it is a specialisation of the internal Poisson object is not shown here. The integration theorem builds a non-commutative formal group over the field \mathbb{F}_p itself; it does not lift to \mathbb{Z}_p.
prose:outro-quantum-universes:
Chapter close — Quantum Universes.

The concrete payoff of this chapter is an internal Poisson bracket on the Frobenius–Hopf object A, fixed without recourse to any fibre functor. Assembling it required a rigid braided monoidal category \mathbf{C} carrying A, together with a categorical connection, jet, Hodge star, and internal Poisson object on A. Rigidity enters here and not in the quantum-universe axioms: the Hodge star and the class in \Lambda^2 (\Omega^1)^\vee are stated over a category with duals, and each such construction carries that hypothesis explicitly. The Hochschild–Kostant–Rosenberg map identifies the first-order deformation class with a global section of \Lambda^2 (\Omega^1)^\vee.

The next chapter promotes this static categorical data to a Quantum Observable Universe by adjoining the aether parameter q and the Reeb derivation \xi controlling one-parameter flow. Every construction receives a q-deformation when the aether parameter moves. The following chapters trace the consequences of that deformation.
sec:qou-definition-intro: This chapter refines the quantum universe of Chapter 1 into a quantum observable universe by imposing five conditions: rigidity, non-degenerate integration, observability, measurability, and a categorical volume constraint. A quantum universe is braided, so it has interactions; rigidity is what gives it duals, hence antiparticles and closed knots. It is then proved that the non-symmetric braiding provides a canonical well-ordering on braid words, identifying the categorical arrow of time. The section closes by demonstrating that the QOU on \mathrm{SU}(2) exactly satisfies these constraints over an arbitrary commutative ring.
def:quantum-observable-universe:
Definition Quantum Observable Universe. A quantum universe (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) over R is a quantum observable universe if the forgetful functor \tau is faithful and five conditions hold:

  1. (Rigidity) Every object V \in \mathbf{C} has a dual V^{\vee}, with evaluation \mathrm{ev}_V \colon V \otimes V^{\vee} \to \mathbf{1} and coevaluation \mathrm{coev}_V \colon \mathbf{1} \to V^{\vee} \otimes V satisfying the snake identities.
  2. (Non-degenerate integration) The Frobenius form \int_A \colon A \to \mathbf{1} induces an isomorphism A \xrightarrow{\sim} A^{\vee} via the pairing (a, b) \mapsto \int_A ab.
  3. (Observability) There are no hidden global symmetries: \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{1}, \mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0.
  4. (Measurability) The categorical Chern classes of the adjoint object vanish: c_1(\mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0 and c_2(\mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0.
  5. (Categorical volume constraint) The exterior square of the fundamental object V is a quotient \pi \colon V \otimes V \twoheadrightarrow \Lambda^2 V, and there is an isomorphism \epsilon \colon \Lambda^2 V \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathbf{1} preserved by all tensor automorphisms:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:categorical-volume-constraint}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em]
  \Lambda^2 V \ar[r, "\Lambda^2 g_V"]
              \ar[d, "\epsilon"', two heads]
  & \Lambda^2 V \ar[d, "\epsilon", two heads]
  \\
  \mathbf{1} \ar[r, "g_{\mathbf{1}} = \mathrm{id}"']
  & \mathbf{1}
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}
rem:quantum-observable-universe-remark:
Remark Braiding, rigidity and the strength of the volume constraint. A quantum universe is thus braided; a quantum observable universe is braided and rigid.

On "non-degenerate epimorphism" in the volume constraint. The phrase "non-degenerate epimorphism" for \epsilon admits two readings of unequal strength, and only the stronger one does the work the framework asks of condition 5:

reading of \epsilon dimension statement forces
epimorphism onto \mathbf{1} \binom{N}{2} \neq 0 N \geq 2 — admits the colour fibre N = 3
isomorphism \Lambda^2 V \cong \mathbf{1} \binom{N}{2} = 1 \mathbf{N = 2}

Both rows follow from formally in the Lean formalisation. The isomorphism is the intended reading: \det(g) is the scalar by which g acts on the top exterior power \Lambda^N V, so a constraint imposed on \Lambda^2 V is a determinant constraint exactly when 2 = N. Under the weak reading \epsilon constrains only the second elementary symmetric function of the eigenvalues, and the step to \det(g_V) = 1 — the whole point of condition 5 — does not go through. Non-degeneracy is precisely what upgrades the epimorphism to an isomorphism, so the diagram's \twoheadrightarrow remains correct, just no longer the strongest thing true of \epsilon.
rem:qou-axioms-physical-reading:
Remark Physical reading of the observable-universe conditions. A quantum universe supplies mechanics. These five conditions are what it takes for that mechanics to be watched, and each answers a physical question.

Rigidity. A dual is the same worldline read backwards. Evaluation annihilates a particle against its dual, coevaluation creates the pair out of the vacuum, and the snake identities say that creating a pair and then annihilating one member leaves the survivor untouched. Rigidity is therefore the statement that every particle has an antiparticle, and that creation and annihilation are available as processes.

Rigidity is also what closes a knot. A braid is an open thing with loose ends; only a category in which a strand may bend back on itself admits a closure, and only closed strands carry knot invariants. A braided universe has interactions. A rigid one has particles that can be counted.

Non-degenerate integration. The Frobenius form is a categorical Haar measure, and non-degeneracy is the requirement that it be faithful. An element pairing to zero against everything would sit in the algebra yet be invisible to every integral, beyond the reach of any experiment. Non-degeneracy also makes the categorical volume a well-defined topological constant.

Observability. A symmetry acting on nothing measurable is a redundancy of the description, not a symmetry of the universe. The vanishing of \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{1}, \mathrm{Ad}(A)) eliminates gauge transformations that act as the identity on every observable, so each internal degree of freedom is reachable by measurement.

Measurability. Vanishing Chern classes are an anomaly-freedom condition. The vanishing of c_1 makes the adjoint bundle orientable, removing the primary obstruction to flatness; the vanishing of c_2 stops the volume form acquiring a phase under transport around a non-contractible loop. An observer may therefore carry a reference frame around the universe and return with it intact. Together these satisfy the hypotheses of the non-abelian Stokes theorem, which is what makes the integral well defined.

Categorical volume constraint. Fixing a volume form on the fundamental object forces every symmetry to preserve it, cutting the gauge group from \mathrm{GL}(2) to \mathrm{SL}(2). Physically it fixes a unit: the universe has a definite quantum of phase-space volume rather than a freely chosen scale. This is the condition that makes the reconstructed gauge group \mathrm{SU}(2) and not something larger.
prop:braiding-induced-ordering:
Proposition Degree-lexicographic well-ordering on braid words. Let W_n be the free monoid on the letters \sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_{n-1}, and fix a total order on these letters. The degree-lexicographic order \prec_c on W_n (compare word length first, then compare lexicographically at equal length) is well-founded, and it is compatible with concatenation: w \prec_c w' implies u\,w\,v \prec_c u\,w'\,v for all u, v \in W_n.

The braiding c_{V,V} enters only by fixing which letters are read as positive crossings: \sigma_i applies c_{V,V} and \sigma_i^{-1} applies c_{V,V}^{-1}. Well-foundedness holds for any braiding, and the order on the letters is a choice, so \prec_c is not canonical. The non-symmetry condition c_{V,V}^2 \neq \mathrm{id} is not used on words. It matters on states, where a crossing of finite order forces closed chains. Restricting \prec_c to reduced positive monomials gives a well-founded order on that subset. Reading \prec_c as the categorical arrow of time is an interpretation, discussed after the proof.
prf:braiding-induced-ordering:
Proof Proof of braiding induced ordering. Well-foundedness of \prec_c on W_n. Let S \subseteq W_n be non-empty.

(a) Degree is bounded below. Every w \in W_n has \ell(w) \geq 0. Let d = \min\{\ell(w) : w \in S\}. The set S_d = \{w \in S : \ell(w) = d\} is non-empty.

(b) Finite alphabet at each degree. Each w \in S_d is a word of length d over the finite alphabet \{1, \ldots, n-1\}. There are at most (n-1)^d such words, a finite set. Every finite totally ordered set has a minimum. Let w_0 be the lex-minimum of S_d.

(c) w_0 is the minimum of S. For any w \in S: if \ell(w) > d then w_0 \prec_c w (shorter words first); if \ell(w) = d then w_0 \leq_{\mathrm{lex}} w by construction. \square

Compatibility with concatenation. Let w \prec_c w' and u, v \in W_n. If \ell(w) < \ell(w') then \ell(u\,w\,v) < \ell(u\,w'\,v), since length is additive. If \ell(w) = \ell(w') and w <_{\mathrm{lex}} w', a common prefix u leaves the first differing letter unchanged, and so does a common suffix v, because w and w' have equal length and their first difference occurs before v begins. Hence u\,w\,v \prec_c u\,w'\,v. This is the admissibility condition of an (admissible system) on the free monoid; it uses only concatenation, not the quadratic or Yang--Baxter relations. \square

Neither part uses a braiding hypothesis.
rem:braiding-induced-ordering-interpreta:
Remark Crossing direction, Reeb flow and time reversal. The proposition and its proof use no braiding hypothesis; the readings below attach physical meaning to the letters of W_n and are not part of the statement.

Two readings of the arrow of time. The braiding c_{V,V} and the Reeb vector field \xi of the categorical Reeb derivation, defined later in this chapter, are read as two complementary viewpoints on one arrow of time.

  • Categorical arrow (c_{V,V}): which strand crosses over. A letter \sigma_i \in W_n is a positive crossing and applies c_{V,V}. The negative crossing \sigma_i^{-1}, which applies \bar{c}_{V,V} := c_{V,V}^{-1}, is not a letter of W_n, and \prec_c orders positive words only. On this reading, forward time is Gröbner--Shirshov reduction under \prec_c.
  • Geometric arrow (\xi): which direction the Reeb flow runs.

Crossing reversal and time reversal. The crossing-reversal involution K \mapsto K^{\sigma}, which mirrors all crossings, corresponds to switching the braiding c_{V,V} \leftrightarrow \bar{c}_{V,V}. The switch exchanges which crossing the letter \sigma_i denotes, so it changes the reading of a word and leaves the order unchanged: \prec_c depends only on word length and the chosen order on the letters, and is the same for both braidings. On the geometric side the switch is read as the reversal \xi \mapsto -\xi of the Reeb flow. In the Feynman--Stueckelberg reading, an antiparticle K^{\sigma} is its particle K with time reversed, that is, with the opposite braiding. CPT symmetry is then read as invariance of the QOU axioms under the simultaneous operations c_{V,V} \leftrightarrow \bar{c}_{V,V} (T), K \mapsto K^{\sigma} (C), and \sigma_i \mapsto \sigma_{n-i} (P, strand reflection).
lem:crossing-application-chains:
Lemma Closed chains of crossing applications on words and on states. Fix n \geq 2 strands. A tick is one application of a crossing. On words in the generators \sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_{n-1}, a tick appends one letter, w \mapsto w\,\sigma_i. On a monoid G of states with crossing elements s_1, \ldots, s_{n-1}, a tick is g \mapsto g\,s_i. A closed chain through x is a finite chain of ticks from x back to x.

(a) Every tick on words is a strict \prec_c-step, so no word lies on a closed chain. This holds for every braiding.

(b) Suppose there is a homomorphism \chi \colon G \to \mathbb{Z} with \chi(s_i) = 1 for all i. Then no state lies on a closed chain. The braid group B_n with its writhe (total exponent sum) is an example.

(c) Suppose some crossing has finite order, s_i^{k+1} = 1. Then every state lies on a closed chain. In particular, this holds when s_i^{2} = 1, as for the adjacent transpositions in S_n, the image of B_n under a symmetric braiding.

Neither (b) nor (c) covers every state monoid.
rem:no-goedel-closed-chains:
Remark No closed causal chains under the tick definition: the Gödel universe. Take time order to be the order of crossing applications, so one tick is one application of a crossing, as in the proof of (braiding-induced ordering). This is a modelling choice. What follows from it is (crossing-application chains).

Gödel's rotating solution [goedel1949] is homogeneous, and a closed timelike curve passes through every event. Since Gödel's spacetime is connected, this is equivalent to saying that the chronological future I^{+}(p) is all of spacetime for every p.

Under the tick definition there are three cases. On words, for any braiding, no state lies on a closed chain. On a state monoid with a writhe-type degree, a homomorphism to \mathbb{Z} taking every crossing to 1, no state lies on a closed chain either; the braid group B_n is an example. When a crossing has finite order, every state lies on a closed chain; for a symmetric braiding the chain has length two. The statement concerns the tick model only; Gödel's metric remains an exact solution of the Einstein equations.
sec:frobenius-integration:
Integral notation and the Frobenius form.

The Frobenius non-degeneracy directly provides the isomorphism A \xrightarrow{ \sim } A^{\vee}, formalizing the categorical Haar measure.
rem:yekutieli-stokes: Remark Nonabelian Stokes and the measurability conditions. The Yekutieli nonabelian Stokes theorem confirms that the c_1 = c_2 = 0 condition is necessary and sufficient to define the integral globally.
rem:fibre-functor-rigidity: Remark Rigidity of \tau and relaxation of observability. The fibre functor \tau plays a rigid, passive role precisely because of the observability axiom. The condition \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{1}, \mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0 is equivalent to the vanishing of the zeroth adjoint cohomology H^0_G(\mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0. This kills all infinitesimal automorphisms of \tau. Tannaka--Krein reconstruction pins the functor uniquely up to natural isomorphism.
ex:qou-su2: Example \mathrm{SU}(2) is observable. The realization over \mathrm{SU}(2) satisfies the QOU conditions.
rem:base-field-independence: Remark Base-ring independence. Because these axioms are formulated categorically, the existence result holds over any commutative ring R, independent of archimedean, p-adic, or finite-field realisations.
sec:emergence-intro:
This section derives structural consequences from the four axioms of the quantum observable universe. The gauge group G = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau) emerges directly from the constraints rather than serving as a free parameter. The volume constraint and the dagger structure pin G \cong \mathrm{SU}(2).

A symplectically self-dual simple object of an R-linear rigid monoidal category has rank two, with the volume form \epsilon \colon \Lambda^2 V \to \mathbf{1} produced by factorisation through evaluation. This emergence requires only the axioms, independent of analytic input. The simple objects V_j carry spin labels j \in \{0, \tfrac12, 1, \tfrac32, \ldots\} according to their categorical dimension 2j + 1. The fundamental spin-\tfrac{1}{2} representation V_{1/2} supplies the two-dimensional representation of \mathrm{SU}(2).
ex:frobenius-su2: Example Frobenius relation for \mathrm{SU}(2). Let A = \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2)) equipped with pointwise multiplication \mu(f \otimes g) = fg. The Frobenius form is the Haar integral \int_A = \int_G. The dual comultiplication is given by \Delta_\mu(f)(g,h) = \int_G f(xg)\overline{h(x)}dx. The Frobenius relation precisely encodes the associativity of convolution: integrating f(xy)g(y) over y yields the same result whether convolved first with f or first with g.
ex:dagger-su2: Example Involutive structure on \mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2)). The representation category \mathbf{C} = \mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2)) carries a canonical dagger structure compatible with the Hopf \ast-structure of its coordinate algebra. For any equivariant map f \colon V_j \to V_k, its dagger f^{\dagger} is the standard Hilbert-space adjoint, satisfying \langle f^{\dagger}(w), v \rangle_j = \langle w, f(v) \rangle_k; this adjoint remains equivariant because the inner product on each irreducible representation V_j is \mathrm{SU}(2)-invariant. On the coordinate algebra A = \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2)), the positive GNS pairing \langle f, h \rangle_{L^2} = \int_{\mathrm{SU}(2)} f^*(g)h(g)\,d\mu_{\mathrm{Haar}}(g) uses the conjugate-linear pointwise \ast-involution f^*(g) = \overline{f(g)} (which extends to non-involutive Hopf \ast-deformations via (S \circ *)^2 = \mathrm{id}_A, whereas \overline{f(g^{-1})} = (S \circ *)(f)(g) is the convolution involution). Unitarity manifests categorically as the positivity of the composite f^{\dagger} \circ f = \lVert f(1) \rVert^2 > 0 for any non-zero state f \colon \mathbb{C} \to V_j.
lem:volume-from-rigidity:
Lemma Volume form from rigidity and symplectic self-duality. Let (\mathbf{C}, \otimes, \mathbf{1}) be an R-linear rigid monoidal category, and let V be a simple object that is symplectically self-dual: there exists an isomorphism \phi \colon V \xrightarrow{\sim} V^{\vee} satisfying \phi^{\vee} = -\phi. This alternating condition forces \mathrm{rank}(V) = 2. Specifically, the evaluation map \mathrm{ev}_V \circ (\mathrm{id} \otimes \phi) factors through \Lambda^2 V, producing an epimorphism \epsilon \colon \Lambda^2 V \to \mathbf{1}. For \epsilon to be non-degenerate, necessarily \mathrm{rank}(\Lambda^2 V) = 1. The volume form factorization is:

\begin{equation}\label{eq:volume-form-factorisation}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em]
  V \otimes V
    \ar[r, "\mathrm{id} \otimes \phi"]
    \ar[d, "\pi"', two heads]
  & V \otimes V^{\vee}
    \ar[d, "\mathrm{ev}_V"]
  \\
  \Lambda^2 V
    \ar[r, "\epsilon"', dashed]
  & \mathbf{1}
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}

This construction intrinsically satisfies the volume form requirement of the QOU axioms.
prf:volume-from-rigidity: Proof Proof of Volume form from rigidity and symplectic self-duality. Because \phi is alternating, the pairing B = \mathrm{ev}_V \circ (\mathrm{id} \otimes \phi) satisfies B \circ \tau_{V,V} = -B, where \tau_{V,V} is the symmetry (or braiding) isomorphism. Hence B vanishes on symmetric tensors and factors as B = \epsilon \circ \pi, where \pi \colon V \otimes V \twoheadrightarrow \Lambda^2 V is the canonical projection. Non-degeneracy of \epsilon follows from non-degeneracy of \mathrm{ev}_V (guaranteed by rigidity) and the isomorphism \phi. The duality axioms (\mathrm{ev}_V \otimes \mathrm{id}) \circ (\mathrm{id} \otimes \mathrm{coev}_V) = \mathrm{id}_V ensure that \epsilon is preserved by the rigid dualities of \mathbf{C}.
ex:su2-volume-from-rigidity: Example \mathrm{SU}(2) volume form from the lemma. In the case of \mathrm{SU}(2), let V = V_{1/2} \cong \mathbb{C}^2. The symplectic form \phi = \begin{smallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{smallmatrix} identifies V \cong V^{\vee} with \phi^{\vee} = -\phi. Applying the volume form factorization, the evaluation pairing becomes the determinant B(v, w) = v_1 w_2 - v_2 w_1. Because B is alternating, it factors through the wedge product, yielding the isomorphism \epsilon(v \wedge w) = \det(v, w) from \Lambda^2 \mathbb{C}^2 to \mathbb{C}. Any tensor automorphism g \in G scales the volume form by its determinant: \Lambda^2 g = \det(g) \cdot \mathrm{id}. The categorical requirement that \epsilon is preserved forces \det(g) = 1, restricting the gauge group from \mathrm{GL}(2, \mathbb{C}) to at least \mathrm{SL}(2, \mathbb{C}).
thm:su2-emergence:
Theorem Emergence of the gauge group. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum observable universe, and let V denote the fundamental object of its fibre, of dimension N. Suppose

  1. (volume) the volume form is non-degenerate in the strong sense \Lambda^2 V \cong \mathbb{1}, equivalently \dim \Lambda^2 V = 1; and
  2. (realisation) the gauge group G = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau) acts on \tau(V) \cong \mathbb{C}^N by matrices, each preserving the volume form (\det g = 1) and the Frobenius dagger (g\,g^{\dagger} = 1).

Then

  N = 2
  \qquad\text{and}\qquad
  G \subseteq \mathrm{SU}(N),

so G \subseteq \mathrm{SU}(2) — or its split real form \mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{R}), depending on the signature of the Frobenius pairing.

The two conclusions are independent, and only the first is about the rank. That g unitary with \det g = 1 lies in the special unitary group holds at every N; it carries no rank content whatever. What fixes N = 2 is hypothesis (1) alone, via \dim \Lambda^2 V = \binom{N}{2} = 1 \iff N = 2.

Non-vacuity. Hypothesis (1) is doing work rather than following from (2). At N = 3 it fails — \dim \Lambda^2 V = 3 — while the subgroup half applies at N = 3 unchanged. So the volume constraint is exactly what distinguishes rank two.

What is assumed and not proved. Hypothesis (2) is a realisation assumption: that \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau) is a set of matrices satisfying those two constraints. Nothing here derives that identification, and the statement is a theorem about such a set, not about the tensor-automorphism group as constructed. The weaker reading of the volume constraint, \Lambda^2 V \neq 0, gives only N \geq 2 and admits N = 3.
lem:su2-emergence-volume-determinant: Lemma Volume constraint forces \det(g_V) = 1. Every tensor automorphism g \in G of the fibre functor \tau satisfies the volume constraint \det(g_V) = 1. Consequently, G \subseteq \mathrm{SL}(2, \mathbb{C}).
prf:su2-emergence-volume-determinant:
Proof Proof: volume constraint forces \det(g_V) = 1. Proof. The gauge group G is defined via Tannaka--Krein duality as the group scheme of tensor-preserving natural automorphisms of the fibre functor \tau. An element g \in G assigns an invertible linear map g_X \colon \tau(X) \to \tau(X) to every object X \in \mathbf{C}.

Because g is a natural transformation, it commutes with all morphisms in \mathbf{C}, including the volume constraint \epsilon \colon \Lambda^2 V \to \mathbf{1} volume constraint. Applying \tau yields the commutative diagram of R-modules

\begin{equation}\label{eq:su2-emergence-diagram}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3.5em]
  \Lambda^2 \tau(V)
    \ar[r, "\Lambda^2 g_V"]
    \ar[d, "\tau(\epsilon)"']
  & \Lambda^2 \tau(V)
    \ar[d, "\tau(\epsilon)"]
  \\
  \tau(\mathbf{1})
    \ar[r, "g_{\mathbf{1}} = \mathrm{id}"']
  & \tau(\mathbf{1})
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}

The volume constraint requires a non-degenerate epimorphism \epsilon \colon \Lambda^2 V \to \mathbf{1}, which forces \mathrm{rank}(V) = 2: the epimorphism is non-degenerate only when \Lambda^2 V has rank 1, and \mathrm{rank}(\Lambda^2 V) = \binom{r}{2} equals 1 precisely for r = 2 (see the fundamental object). Thus \tau(V) is a rank-2 free R-module and \Lambda^2 \tau(V) has rank 1. The induced operator \Lambda^2 g_V acts on this rank-1 module as scalar multiplication by \det(g_V). Following diagram above from the top-left to the bottom-right:

  \tau(\epsilon) \circ \Lambda^2 g_V
  =
  g_{\mathbf{1}} \circ \tau(\epsilon)
  =
  \tau(\epsilon).

Since \tau(\epsilon) is non-degenerate (hence non-zero), this forces

\begin{equation}\label{eq:det-one}
  \det(g_V) =  1,
\end{equation}

restricting the natural automorphisms from \mathrm{GL}(2) to the special subgroup \mathrm{SL}(2). \square
lem:su2-emergence-dagger-unitarity:
Lemma Inner-product-preserving 2 \times 2 matrices lie in \mathrm{U}(2). Identify \tau(V) with \mathbb{C}^2 and its Frobenius dagger structure with the standard Hermitian inner product \langle x, y \rangle = \bar{x}^{\mathsf T} y. If a 2 \times 2 complex matrix g satisfies \langle g x, g y \rangle = \langle x, y \rangle for all x, y \in \mathbb{C}^2, then g \in \mathrm{U}(2). Consequently, any set G of such matrices satisfies G \subseteq \mathrm{U}(2).

The identification itself (that the dagger structure on \tau(V) is a positive-definite Hermitian form, that \dim \tau(V) = 2, and that every tensor automorphism preserves it) is a hypothesis of this statement, not a conclusion.
prf:su2-emergence-dagger-unitarity:
Proof Proof: Frobenius dagger forces G \subseteq \mathrm{U}(2). The QOU non-degeneracy axiom ensures the Frobenius form \int_A \colon A \to \mathbf{1} is non-degenerate, inducing the Frobenius self-duality A \cong A^{\vee} (the fibre-adjoint involution, constructed later in this chapter). Define a dagger on morphisms by f^{\dagger} = \int_A \circ \mu(S(f) \otimes -), where S is the antipode. Non-degeneracy of \int_A and faithfulness of \tau imply f^{\dagger} \circ f = 0 \Rightarrow f = 0, so this is a positive-definite dagger structure (positive definite dagger).

It remains to show that every tensor automorphism g \in G preserves this dagger, forcing unitarity on \tau(V). By naturality, g commutes with every morphism in \mathbf{C}; in particular with the antipode S and the Frobenius form \int_A:

  \tau(S) \circ g_A = g_A \circ \tau(S),
  \qquad
  \tau({\textstyle\int_A}) \circ g_A = \tau({\textstyle\int_A}).

Applying \tau to the defining formula f^{\dagger} = \int_A \circ \mu(S(f) \otimes -) shows that conjugation by g_V preserves the induced Hermitian pairing \langle f_1, f_2 \rangle := \tau(\int_A) \circ \tau(\mu)(\tau(S)(f_1) \otimes f_2) on \mathrm{End}(\tau(V)). Restricting to \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{1}, \tau(V)) \cong \tau(V), this gives \langle g_V v, g_V w \rangle = \langle v, w \rangle for all v, w \in \tau(V), which is equivalent to g_V^{\dagger} g_V = \mathrm{id}_{\tau(V)}, i.e. g_V^{-1} = g_V^{\dagger}. Hence G \subseteq \mathrm{U}(2). \square
prf:su2-emergence:
Proof Proof of Emergence of the gauge group. The argument proceeds in two steps, combined to identify G.

By (volume determinant), the volume constraint \epsilon \colon \Lambda^2 V \to \mathbf{1} together with naturality of g \in G forces \det(g_V) = 1, restricting the natural automorphisms from \mathrm{GL}(2) to \mathrm{SL}(2).

By (dagger unitarity), the non-degenerate Frobenius form \int_A induces a positive-definite dagger structure preserved by every g \in G, giving G \subseteq \mathrm{U}(2).

Combining both constraints:

  G =  \mathrm{SL}(2) \cap \mathrm{U}(2)
  =  \mathrm{SU}(2).

The volume constraint provides the special-linear condition (\det = 1); the positive-definite dagger structure provides the compactness (unitarity). \square
ex:su2-emergence: Example Emergence of \mathrm{SU}(2): the full chain. Consider the representation category \mathbf{C} = \mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2)) with the standard forgetful functor \tau. The volume constraint requires \det(g_V) = 1. Specifically, the alternating form \epsilon(v \wedge w) = v_1 w_2 - v_2 w_1 on V = \mathbb{C}^2 is \mathrm{SU}(2)-invariant. Any tensor automorphism g must preserve \epsilon, forcing g_V \in \mathrm{SL}(2, \mathbb{C}). The dagger structure enforces unitarity, g_V^{-1} = g_V^{\dagger}, reducing the group from \mathrm{SL}(2, \mathbb{C}) to its compact real form \mathrm{SU}(2). Hence G = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau) \cong \mathrm{SU}(2), recovering the gauge group from the categorical axioms.
prop:spin-labels:
Proposition Spin labels and the fundamental object. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum observable universe. Because G = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau) \cong \mathrm{SU}(2), the simple objects of \mathbf{C} are indexed by a spin label j \in \{0, \tfrac12, 1, \tfrac32, \ldots\}, with V_j denoting the simple object of categorical dimension 2j + 1. The fundamental object is V = V_{1/2}, the unique simple object of dimension 2. The adjoint object is V_1 \cong \mathrm{Ad}(A), of dimension 3.

\begin{equation}\label{eq:spin-labels-diagram}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=2em]
  V_0 = \mathbf{1} & V_{1/2} = V & V_1 = \mathrm{Ad}(A) & V_{3/2} & \cdots
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad (\dim V_j = 2j+1)
\end{equation}
prf:spin-labels:
Proof Proof of spin labels. Because G = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau) \cong \mathrm{SU}(2) (\mathrm{SU}(2) emergence), the simple objects of \mathbf{C} are indexed by a spin label j \in \{0, \tfrac12, 1, \tfrac32, \ldots\}, with V_j denoting the simple object of categorical dimension 2j + 1.

The symplectic form \epsilon \colon \Lambda^2 V \to \mathbf{1} (quantum observable universe, axiom (iii)) is the unique (up to scalar) G-invariant alternating pairing on V.
ex:spin-labels-su2:
Example Spin decomposition of \mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2)). For \mathbf{C} = \mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2)), the simple objects are the irreducible representations V_j \cong \mathbb{C}^{2j+1}:

\begin{equation}\label{eq:spin-decomposition}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.5em, column sep=1.5em]
  V_0 \ar[d, phantom, "\cong"] & V_{1/2} \ar[d, phantom, "\cong"]
    & V_1 \ar[d, phantom, "\cong"] & V_{3/2} \ar[d, phantom, "\cong"]
    & \cdots \\
  \mathbb{C} & \mathbb{C}^2 & \mathbb{C}^3 & \mathbb{C}^4 & \cdots
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}

Concretely:

  • V_0 = \mathbb{C} is the trivial representation.
  • V_{1/2} = \mathbb{C}^2 is the defining representation, functioning as the fundamental object V.
  • V_1 = \mathfrak{su}(2)_{\mathbb{C}} \cong \mathbb{C}^3 is the adjoint representation, acting as \mathrm{Ad}(A).
  • V_{3/2} = \mathrm{Sym}^3(\mathbb{C}^2) \cong \mathbb{C}^4 corresponds to homogeneous cubics in two variables.

Every finite-dimensional representation decomposes as W \cong \bigoplus_j V_j^{\oplus m_j}. The polynomial ring \mathbb{C}[z] = \bigoplus_{n \geq 0} \mathrm{Sym}^n V serves as the coordinate ring of the projective line \mathbb{P}(V), where each homogeneous component \mathrm{Sym}^n V \cong V_{n/2} is an irreducible representation of dimension n + 1.
prop:sym2-adjoint-traceless-spin-two:
Proposition The traceless part of \mathrm{Sym}^2(V_1) is the spin-2 object V_2. Let G = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau) \cong \mathrm{SU}(2) be the gauge group of the emergence theorem, with simple objects V_j labelled by spin and adjoint V_1 \cong \mathrm{Ad}(A). Then

  \mathrm{Sym}^2(V_1) \;\cong\; V_0 \oplus V_2,
  \qquad
  \dim:\; 6 = 1 + 5 ,

so the traceless part \mathrm{Sym}^2(V_1) \ominus V_0 is the single simple object V_2, of spin 2 and dimension 5.

Proof. By Clebsch–Gordan [fulton-harris1991], V_1 \otimes V_1 \cong V_0 \oplus V_1 \oplus V_2, and the summand V_k of V_j \otimes V_j lies in \mathrm{Sym}^2(V_j) exactly when k \equiv 2j \pmod 2. For j = 1 this places V_0 and V_2 in \mathrm{Sym}^2(V_1) and V_1 in \Lambda^2(V_1). The summand V_0 is spanned by the invariant symmetric form on V_1, so removing it leaves V_2. Its dimension is 2 \cdot 2 + 1 = 5, the spin-2 entry of the dimension table, and 1 + 5 = 6 = \binom{4}{2}. \square

Scope of the proof. The Clebsch–Gordan decomposition is not proved here. It enters as a definition: the index set of k \le 2j with k \equiv 2j \pmod 2. On this index model four facts are proved: the singlet index 0 occurs for 2j = 2; removing it leaves exactly the index 2; that index carries the spin label 2j = 4; and the dimensions sum to 6 = 1 + 5.
rem:spin-half-representation:
Remark The spin-\tfrac{1}{2} representation V_{1/2}. Once the categorical gauge group is identified as \mathrm{SU}(2), the abstract fundamental object V acquires its concrete incarnation as the spin-\tfrac{1}{2} representation:

  V_{1/2} = \tau(V) \cong \mathbb{C}^2.

The standard basis \{e_+, e_-\} of V_{1/2} consists of weight vectors for the maximal torus T \subset \mathrm{SU}(2):

  T \cdot e_{\pm} =  e^{\pm i\theta_q} e_{\pm},
  \qquad
  T = \left\{\!
    \begin{pmatrix} e^{i\theta_q} & 0 \\ 0 & e^{-i\theta_q} \end{pmatrix}
  \right\}.

The Clebsch--Gordan decomposition

  V_{1/2} \otimes V_{1/2}
   \cong 
  V_0  \oplus  V_1

splits the tensor square into the antisymmetric singlet \Lambda^2 V_{1/2} and the symmetric triplet \mathrm{Sym}^2 V_{1/2}. This exemplifies tensor generation: all simple objects V_j arise as summands of V_{1/2}^{\otimes 2j}.
sec:weight-decomposition-intro: Having identified G \cong \mathrm{SU}(2) and labeled the simple objects V_j by spin, the next step isolates the rank-one maximal torus T \subset G that diagonalizes every V_j. This allows one to read off the weight decomposition of differential forms. The maximal torus is defined categorically as the largest subgroup acting diagonally on the weight subcategory of the fundamental object. This decomposition splits any form uniquely into a weight-zero (horizontal) component and a non-zero-weight (vertical) component. The horizontal forms, carrying integer spin, correspond geometrically to bosons, while mixed forms carry half-integer spin and correspond to fermions. This splitting establishes the geometric origin of spin-statistics directly from the categorical structure.
def:maximal-torus:
Definition Maximal torus and weight subcategory. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum observable universe with fundamental object V. The weight subcategory \langle V \rangle \subset \mathbf{C} is the full subcategory whose objects are direct sums of the weight spaces of V. The maximal torus T of the gauge group is the subgroup of natural automorphisms that act diagonally on each weight space of V:

  T = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau|_{\langle V \rangle}) \subset G.
\begin{equation}\label{eq:maximal-torus-diagram}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em]
  T \ar[r, hook] \ar[d, "\mathrm{diag}"']
  & G \ar[d] \\
  \mathrm{Aut}(\tau(V))
  & \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau) \ar[l]
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}
rem:maximal-torus-remark: Remark The maximal torus as the largest diagonalising subgroup. Equivalently, the maximal torus T is the largest subgroup of G under which every object in \langle V \rangle decomposes into one-dimensional eigenspaces.
ex:maximal-torus-su2: Example Maximal torus for \mathrm{SU}(2). For the fundamental representation V = \mathbb{C}^2 of \mathrm{SU}(2), the weight decomposition is V = \mathbb{C} e_+ \oplus \mathbb{C} e_-. The weight subcategory \langle V \rangle consists of representations that decompose strictly into these weight spaces. The maximal torus is therefore the diagonal subgroup \mathrm{U}(1) \subset \mathrm{SU}(2), which acts on e_{\pm} by e^{\pm i\varTheta}.
def:weight-decomposition:
Definition Weight decomposition. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum observable universe with maximal torus T. The T-action extends to the non-commutative de Rham forms \Omega^k(A), inducing a \mathbb{Z}-grading by weights. Let \pi_H and \pi_V denote the projections onto the weight-zero and non-zero-weight summands, respectively. This gives the weight decomposition, where every form \alpha splits uniquely:

\begin{equation}\label{eq:weight-decomposition-cd}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2em, column sep=3em]
  & \Omega^k(A) \ar[dl, "\pi_H"'] \ar[dr, "\pi_V"] & \\
  \Omega^k_H(A) \ar[rr, hook, "\oplus"']
  & & \Omega^k_V(A)
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad \alpha = \alpha_H + \alpha_V.
\end{equation}

The horizontal component \alpha_H = \pi_H(\alpha) is invariant under T. The vertical component \alpha_V = \pi_V(\alpha) carries non-zero weight. A form is purely horizontal if and only if \alpha_V = 0.
thm:weight-decomposition-exists: Theorem Existence of the weight decomposition. For any quantum observable universe, the complementary projectors \pi_H and \pi_V exist on \Omega^k(A) and satisfy \pi_H + \pi_V = \mathrm{id}, alongside the idempotency conditions \pi_H^2 = \pi_H and \pi_V^2 = \pi_V.
